title: The Hidden Cost of Always being Available
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that leaders who make themselves permanently reachable end up undervalued, exhausted and less effective. She opens with a late-night scene of an empathic professional pulled into email after hours, then reframes constant availability as a trap that resets the norm and lowers one's perceived worth. She draws on Emotional Intelligence 2.0 for the case that protected think-time produces better decisions, and she insists that declining an ad-hoc call is legitimate. A personal anecdote about a 4:53 pm ping shows how a short, courteous message can set a boundary without damaging the relationship. The piece closes by treating boundary-setting as an act of self-management and empathy, not selfishness.
points: Being always available becomes the expected norm, so the habit lowers rather than raises how much a person is valued.
Blocking at least fifteen undistracted minutes a day to think, per Bradberry and Greaves, protects decisions from emotional drift.
Declining an unplanned 'got a minute' request is defensible because answering while distracted serves the colleague poorly.
The boundary script in the Chad example is brief and factual, showing that clarity about working hours need not sound curt.
The author treats boundary-setting as a self-management skill that a leader models for the team.
quotes: The premise is that having at least 15 minutes a day without distractions to think and problem-solve is a great way to ensure that your decisions are made without the impact of emotions swaying you the wrong way.
Politely decline and say you do not have time because you don't. You need to spend your time recalibrating and problem-solving with a clear mind.
Hey Chad, I was away from my computer when you pinged. A reminder: I usually am online during Central Time hours, not Pacific time. How can I help?
Would you rather have an efficient 45 hours of work in a week vs. a less productive 60 hours? If you are a leader, what would you prefer from your team?
Setting boundaries does not make you a jerk. Actually, it's empathic of you to be open with others and kind to yourself with your needs.
